records.query: Need the patient's echocardiography and electrocardiogram results, along with cardiac biomarkers such as BNP or troponin, to confirm or exclude cardiac causes of exertional dyspnea; these are core examinations for evaluating cardiac structure, function, and ischemia.
records.text:
Laboratory tests: Elevated blood glucose level. Basic metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and B-type natriuretic peptide levels were within normal limits.

ECG Studies: 
  1. Resting 12-lead ECG: Normal sinus rhythm with narrow QRS complexes (80 milliseconds)
  2. Exercise Treadmill Test ECG findings: 
    Image Title: Selected 12-Lead ECGs Recorded During Exercise Treadmill Test
    Image Description: 
     - At rest: QRS duration 80 milliseconds
     - During Bruce stage 1: QRS duration increased from 100 to 136 milliseconds with wide-QRS-complex morphology
     - Recovery period: QRS duration decreased from 152 to 80 milliseconds
     - End of recovery: QRS duration 80 milliseconds with new T-wave inversions in lead V3

Echocardiogram findings: 
  - Normal left and right ventricular size and function
  - Left ventricular ejection fraction >60%
  - No wall motion abnormalities
  - Sclerotic aortic valve
  - Mild mitral regurgitation
  - Mild-to-moderate tricuspid regurgitation
  - Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 35 mm Hg.

records.query: Need the patient's coronary angiography or myocardial perfusion imaging results (core examinations for confirming or excluding coronary artery disease as the cause of exercise-induced ischemia).

Need the patient's coronary angiography or myocardial perfusion imaging results explicitly, as the prior retrieval returned no data; these are the core examinations to confirm or exclude coronary artery disease as the cause of exercise-induced ischemia and verify the leading hypothesis.

Need the patient's coronary angiography or stress myocardial perfusion imaging results to definitively confirm or exclude obstructive coronary artery disease, as the exercise ECG findings of dynamic QRS widening and new T-wave inversions strongly suggest ischemia but require anatomical or perfusion correlation.

Need the patient's coronary angiography or stress myocardial perfusion imaging results; previous retrieval yielded no data, and these are essential to confirm or exclude obstructive coronary artery disease given the ischemic exercise ECG findings.

Need coronary CT angiography or invasive coronary angiography results to directly confirm or exclude coronary artery disease; this is the core imaging evidence that would verify the exercise-induced ischemic ECG changes, since prior perfusion imaging requests returned no data and BNP/echo only rule out heart failure.

Need the patient's coronary angiography or myocardial perfusion imaging report, as prior retrieval returned no data; this is the only missing core evidence to confirm or exclude coronary artery disease and verify the exercise-induced ischemic ECG changes.

Need the patient's coronary CT angiography or cardiac MRI perfusion results; prior requests for invasive angiography and SPECT MPI yielded no data, and either would provide the anatomical or perfusion correlation essential to confirm exercise-induced myocardial ischemia and rule out non-obstructive causes.

Need the patient's detailed cardiovascular risk factor profile and symptom history (including hypertension, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia, family history, and any chest discomfort) to refine pretest probability for coronary artery disease, as coronary angiography and perfusion imaging remain unavailable.

bindings.label: Worsening dyspnea on exertion for 2 months
65-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity
Medications included lisinopril, aspirin, and atorvastatin
Physical examination showed vital signs within normal limits and unremarkable cardiac and respiratory examinations
Echocardiography shows preserved LVEF without wall motion abnormalities
Exercise ECG shows dynamic QRS widening and new T-wave inversions in recovery
Echocardiography shows sclerotic aortic valve with mild regurgitation
Exertional dyspnea is caused by coronary artery disease with exercise-induced myocardial ischemia
Coronary angiography or myocardial perfusion imaging was requested but no results are available
Aortic valve sclerosis with mild regurgitation contributes to exertional dyspnea
Coronary artery disease with exercise-induced myocardial ischemia
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
Aortic valve sclerosis with hemodynamically significant regurgitation as primary cause
Positron emission tomography showed increased uptake in the left adrenal gland with a standardized uptake value of 7.4
